intro: To export a presentation as a PDF in Keynote on Mac, open the file and choose File > Export To > PDF. Set your options, click Save, name the file, pick a location and click Export.
tldr: Open the presentation in Keynote and choose File > Export To > PDF.
Tick the options you need, such as presenter notes or comments, then click Save.
Name the file, choose where it goes in the Where menu, and click Export.
Need more control? Use File > Print, then the PDF menu at the bottom of the dialog.
Keyboard: Command-P opens Print and Command-S saves. Apple lists no export shortcut.

blocks.text: This guide covers the Keynote app on a Mac. Keynote for iCloud runs in a browser and has its own steps, which I cover further down. Most people need only the File menu route, so start there.
Check your Keynote and macOS versions first

Choose Keynote > About Keynote from the menu bar to see your version number. Apple's What's New page lists Keynote 15.4 as the newest release. It requires macOS 26 or later. If your Mac runs an older system, you cannot install that release, and your menus may look different.

Apple's export page does not name a Keynote or macOS version. The labels in this guide follow Apple's wording. If a label has moved on your Mac, look for the closest match in the export sheet and keep going.
Export a presentation as a PDF from the File menu

Open the presentation and save any last edits first. Keynote exports whatever is in the open file. Then choose File > Export To > PDF. The export sheet opens with a set of options. Most of them can stay as they are.
Keynote PDF export options, one by one
The sheet decides what goes into the PDF. Here is what each control does, based on Apple's list for the Mac app.

items: Presenter notes and skipped slides: adds your speaker notes and any slides you hid for the show.
Print each stage of builds: gives each build step its own page, so the PDF shows the stages in order.
Include comments: keeps the comments from your slides in the file.
Image Quality: a pop-up menu. Higher quality keeps photos sharp but makes the file bigger.
Advanced Options: set accessibility tags for large tables to On if your deck has big tables.
Require password to open: appears in some releases. Set one if the deck holds sensitive figures.

blocks.text: Match the options to the reader. A handout for people who missed the talk usually needs presenter notes. A file for a printer often works better with builds turned off, so each slide prints once.
Presenter notes cause the most surprise. If the notes are missing from your PDF, the box was off. Tick it and export again. An export creates a new file, so the presentation itself stays as it was.
Save, name and place the PDF file

Click Save when the options look right. Keynote asks for a name. Type one and leave off the .pdf extension, because Keynote adds it. You can add tags too, which help you find the file later in Finder.

Open the Where pop-up menu and choose a folder. Desktop and Documents are the usual picks. Click Export. Keynote writes the file and closes the sheet. Open the PDF in Preview and check it before you send it anywhere.
Print to PDF in Keynote on Mac for more control
The print route gives you the same kind of PDF with more layout choices. Start with File > Print. Then pick a print format: Slide, Grid, Handout or Outline.

Click the PDF pop-up menu at the bottom of the print dialog and choose an option. Then click Print. Apple does not list the labels in that menu, so the names on your Mac may differ. Pick the option that saves a file rather than sending it to a printer.

Want the extra export options from the sheet? Click Cancel in the export sheet. Then choose File > Print and click Show Details at the bottom of the print dialog. Apple's steps say this gives you more PDF options.
For slides as they look on screen, choose the Slide layout. Select Include comments in that layout if the comments should print. Command-P opens the print dialog, and Command-S saves the file first.
Export a PDF from Keynote for iCloud in a browser

Open the presentation in Keynote for iCloud. Click the More button, the one with three dots, in the toolbar. Choose Download a Copy, then select PDF. From the document manager, select the presentation, click More, then choose Download a Copy.

Shared presentations set to View Only use the Download button in the toolbar instead. Files save to your browser's download location. In Safari, you can check that location under Safari > Settings > General.
Apple's browser page does not list the PDF options it offers, so do not assume the Mac options are there. For presenter notes or accessibility tags, export from the Mac app instead.
Keep the file small, readable and accessible
Image Quality is the setting people change by accident. Pick a lower setting for email and a higher one for print. Then check the file size in Finder, because the setting changes it.
Advanced Options matters if your slides have large tables. Turn on accessibility tags for large tables, so screen readers can make sense of them. Charts need a separate check, covered below.

Password protection shows up only in some releases. Use it when the deck holds pricing, client names or plans nobody should see yet. Store the password somewhere safe, because the PDF will not open without it.
Fix the export problems people report
Most exports finish with no trouble. A few problems come up again and again in Apple's community forums. The fixes below come from those threads, not from Apple, so test them on a copy first.

Long decks can crash during export. One report describes a presentation of 200 pages that crashed on a MacBook Air running macOS 12.4. Suggested fixes include freeing disk space, deleting the partial PDF, and relaunching with Shift held. The thread does not confirm that any of them worked.

Charts can lose their labels. A separate thread reports that Keynote 14.3 on macOS 15.1 dropped chart data labels and values in PDF export. The poster said exporting charts as images avoids the error, but that makes the PDF inaccessible to screen readers. No Apple employee replied.

blocks.text: A worked example: exporting a client deck
Say you have a sales deck for a client. It has speaker notes they should read, a chart with last quarter's results, and a few hidden backup slides. The client wants a PDF they can open on a phone.

Start with File > Export To > PDF. Tick Presenter notes and skipped slides, so the notes and backup slides come along. Leave Print each stage of builds off, since the client needs the final state of each slide.

Lower the Image Quality, because a phone screen does not need print detail. Click Save, name the file with the client and the date, then export. Open the PDF on your phone and check the chart labels before you send it.
Now the printer copy. Choose File > Print, pick Slide layout, open the PDF menu and choose the option that saves a file. Include comments only if the printer proof needs them.
Mistakes people make when they export
The first mistake is exporting before the last edit. Keynote does not wait for you. Press Command-S, then export, so the PDF matches the slides on your screen.
The second is assuming notes come along. They do only when Presenter notes and skipped slides is ticked. Check the box every time you export a deck that has notes.
The third is trusting the file without opening it. Check the page count, the hidden slides and every chart. A file that looks fine on the first page can hide a missing label further in.
The fourth is using the browser route for a job that needs Mac options. The browser is quick, but Apple does not document its dialog options. Use the Mac app for anything detailed.
What to do after the PDF is saved
Name the file with the deck title, the date and the version, so the right copy reaches the right person. Then send it, or upload it to the place where your team keeps finished files.
A PDF is a flat file. Transitions and animations do not play the way they do in Keynote, so present from the Keynote file if motion matters. Use the PDF for sharing and printing.

For notes, see [how to add presenter notes in Keynote](/how-to/add-presenter-notes-in-keynote). If you need a movie instead, read [how to export a Keynote presentation as a movie on Mac](/how-to/export-a-presentation-as-a-movie-in-keynote).

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut to export a Keynote presentation as a PDF?
faq.answer: Apple's shortcut list does not include an export shortcut. The closest route is Command-P to open Print, then the PDF menu at the bottom of the dialog. Command-S saves the presentation first, which is a good habit before any export.

faq.question: Why are my speaker notes missing from the PDF?
faq.answer: Notes export only when Presenter notes and skipped slides is ticked in the export sheet. Tick it, click Save, and export again. Your original presentation stays as it was.

faq.question: Which macOS version does Keynote 15.4 need?
faq.answer: Apple's What's New page says Keynote 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later. To check your version, open the Apple menu, choose About This Mac, and read the macOS name and number.

faq.question: Can I export only some of the slides?
faq.answer: Apple's export steps do not describe a page range. Make a copy of the file in Finder, open the copy, delete the slides you do not want, then export the copy. Your original deck stays complete.

faq.question: Does Keynote for iCloud export the same PDF as the Mac app?
faq.answer: Apple does not list the PDF dialog options for Keynote for iCloud, so you cannot assume the same settings exist. Use Download a Copy for a quick file. Use the Mac app when you need presenter notes or accessibility tags.

faq.question: Why is my PDF so large?
faq.answer: Image Quality controls how big the images are. Higher settings keep photos sharp but make the file bigger. Lower the setting for email, then check the file size in Finder.

task: Export a Keynote presentation as a PDF on Mac
appliesTo: Keynote for Mac 15.4 (per Apple's What's New), macOS 26 or later

steps.name: Open the presentation
steps.text: Open the Keynote file on your Mac. Press Command-S first so the file on disk matches what you see. Check the slides once more, especially any hidden or backup slides.
steps.tip: Save before you export. The PDF only includes what is in the open file.

steps.name: Open the export menu
steps.text: Choose File > Export To > PDF from the menu bar. Keynote opens the export sheet with its PDF options.

steps.name: Tick the options you need
steps.text: Turn on Presenter notes and skipped slides if your audience needs notes or hidden slides. Turn on Include comments if the comments should appear. Leave Print each stage of builds off for a handout, or turn it on to show each build.
steps.tip: If a label is unclear, check the option list earlier in this guide.

steps.name: Click Save
steps.text: Click Save in the export sheet. Keynote moves to the naming step, where you give the file its name.

steps.name: Name the file and choose a location
steps.text: Type a name without the .pdf extension. Add tags if you want them. Open the Where pop-up menu and pick a folder, such as Desktop or Documents.
steps.tip: Pick a name with the deck title and the date, so you can find the right copy later.

steps.name: Click Export and check the file
steps.text: Click Export. Keynote writes the PDF to the folder you chose. Open it in Preview and scroll through every page, including charts and notes.
steps.tip: Keep the presentation open until Keynote finishes writing the file.

troubleshooting.problem: Keynote crashes during a long export
troubleshooting.fix: Community suggestions include freeing disk space, deleting the partial PDF, relaunching with Shift held, and splitting the deck to find the slide that fails. Apple has not confirmed these, so test on a copy.

troubleshooting.problem: Chart labels are missing in the PDF
troubleshooting.fix: One thread reports this in Keynote 14.3 on macOS 15.1. Exporting charts as images avoids it, but the PDF becomes inaccessible to screen readers. Check every chart in Preview before you send the file.

troubleshooting.problem: Speaker notes are missing from the PDF
troubleshooting.fix: Open File > Export To > PDF, tick Presenter notes and skipped slides, then click Save and export again.

troubleshooting.problem: The PDF menu in the print dialog has different names
troubleshooting.fix: Apple does not list the labels in that menu. Choose the option that saves a file to disk rather than sending it to a printer, then open the result in Preview.

troubleshooting.problem: The PDF file is too large
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the Image Quality setting in the export sheet. Higher quality makes the file bigger, so check the size in Finder after each export.

troubleshooting.problem: Keynote for iCloud has no Download a Copy option
troubleshooting.fix: Click the More button, the one with three dots, in the toolbar. For a shared presentation set to View Only, use the Download button in the toolbar instead.
